### B.10 Every presented ordinary character

Let a Hecke character in modulus $\mathfrak m$ be induced by the primitive $\eta^*$ of conductor $\mathfrak f\mid\mathfrak m$. Absolute Euler products on $\Re s>1$ give

$$
L_{\mathfrak m}(s,\eta)=L(s,\eta^*)
 \prod_{\substack{p\mid\mathfrak m\\p\nmid\mathfrak f}}
                 (1-\eta^*(p)q_p^{-s}).
$$

Continuation extends this identity away from the principal pole. Each deleted factor is nonzero for $\Re s>0$ since $|\eta^*(p)q_p^{-s}|<1$. Thus primitive reduction and fixed-$S$ restoration preserve zeros. Reflected numerator bounds [(221)](#dr:rowmass)–[(222)](#dr:mass) still retain repeated row powers/holes.

For any $q\ge1$ and complex Dirichlet $\chi\bmod q$, norm pullback $\eta_\chi(\mathfrak a)=\chi(N\mathfrak a)$ has finite order in modulus $q\mathcal O$ and is trivial on units. Let $\chi_{-3}$ be the field character and present $\chi\chi_{-3}$ at a common modulus. Euler factors give

<a id="dr:norm-lift"></a>

$$
L_K(s,\eta_\chi)=L(s,\chi)L(s,\chi\chi_{-3}).
 \qquad\text{(240)}
$$

Split primes give two norm-$p$ factors with $\chi_{-3}(p)=1$; inert primes give a norm-$p^2$ factor equal to the product with signs $\pm$. Prime three gives one factor and $\chi_{-3}(3)=0$. At $p\mid q$ all corresponding factors are deleted. This proves [(240)](#dr:norm-lift) absolutely, then by continuation.

For $\theta<\Re s<1$, both Dirichlet factors are holomorphic, so a zero contradicts Hecke nonvanishing. For $\Re s\ge1$ use ordinary Dirichlet nonvanishing, excepting the principal pole; treat nonprincipal $s=1$ directly even if its companion is principal. Thus every presented modulus and finite height satisfy

$$
\Re s>\theta,\qquad
 \neg(\chi=1\ \hbox{and}\ s=1)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(s,\chi)\ne0.
$$

Modulus-one principal gives zeta. This transfer asserts no boundary-line or growing-modulus uniformity.

## Appendix C. Complete restoration and source assembly

The proofs in this appendix discharge the specialized source obligations
used in §4. Their order follows the operations: finite projectors and the
whole-column transfer; a reference bound; the first exact physical source;
masked packing and cube-free restoration; the joint divisor budget; then
the diagonal and complete generic assembly. The selected-norm foundation
of §3 only enters the new leaf price. It does not replace any of these
complementary arguments.

Numbered equations in each C.1–C.10 module are local to that module;
an external citation names the module, for example C.8(16). The older named
equation families are preserved where they are already unambiguous; the correspondence table
at the end of the manuscript records their local locations. No historical
cycle or catalogue fetch is required to follow these proofs.


### C.1. Finite projectors and normalized restoring mass


This section gives the local identities and absolute coefficient bounds used
in the fourth-power source construction. It uses the Eisenstein ideal
conventions of Appendix A.1–A.2. A supported ideal is nonzero and prime to the
primes above 2 and 3; a supported prime has norm at least 7. All characters
retain their zero values at nonunits. The results concern the actual common
coefficient families; none asserts a bound for arbitrary row-dependent
coefficients.

The restriction on an ordinary pair is
\(v_{\mathfrak p}(n_1)+v_{\mathfrak p}(n_2)<5\) at every supported prime.
This is a restriction on the product, not two separate fifth-free conditions.
A live marked prime is also excluded from both ordinary factors. Initially
the live marks are distinct. Repeated marks will be restored by the exact
equality-pattern decomposition below.

##### 1. Local identities before norms

In the formal series ring in two variables put
\[
 O=(1-x)^{-1}(1-y)^{-1},\qquad B=(1-x)(1-y),\qquad
 T_4=\sum_{i+j<5}x^iy^j.
\]
Then
\[
 H=BT_4=1-\sum_{i+j=5}x^iy^j+xy\sum_{i+j=4}x^iy^j,
 \qquad R=H^{-1}.
 \tag{VII.2.1}
\]
The inverse exists formally because the constant coefficient of H is one.
The nonconstant part has six terms of degree five and five of degree six.
Direct multiplication gives
\[
 HO=T_4,\qquad RT_4=O.
 \tag{VII.2.2}
\]
Introduce a mark variable z with \(z^2=0\). The unrestricted local state is
\(O+zO\): a marked prime can occur in the ordinary factors. The restricted
state is \(T_4+z\): when the prime is marked, both ordinary valuations are
zero. The two exact identities are
\[
 [H+z(B-H)](O+zO)=T_4+z,
\]
\[
 [R+z(H-B)R^2](T_4+z)=O+zO.
 \tag{VII.2.3}
\]
These follow from BO=1 and (VII.2.2). In particular the marked coefficient
in the restricted state is 1, not T_4. Replacing it by T_4 gives the wrong
coefficient already at the monomial \(x^2z\) in the inverse identity.

For finitely many distinct marked primes use separate nilpotent variables,
and take the coefficient of their product after multiplying (VII.2.3) over
a finite enclosing prime set. This is a finite ideal-divisor convolution
at every fixed ordinary pair. Formal series cause no interchange problem:
only finitely many terms can contribute to any fixed valuation vector.

Here is the reindexing that will be used analytically. Let D be a finite
ordinary-pair set, k an extraction coefficient and r a residual coefficient.
Complete multiplicativity, including nonunit zeros, gives
\[
 \sum_{n\in D}\ \sum_{d_1\mid n_1,d_2\mid n_2}
 k(d)r(n/d)\chi(n_1n_2)f(n)
 =\sum_d k(d)\chi(d_1d_2)
       \sum_{a:\,da\in D}r(a)\chi(a_1a_2)f(da).
 \tag{VII.2.4}
\]
The outer sum is over the divisor pool of D. No character value is divided
out. For a normalized row with ordinary scales X_1,X_2, the residual scales
are exactly \(X_1/Nd_1,X_2/Nd_2\), and the outside scalar is
\[
 k(d)\chi(d_1d_2)/\sqrt{Nd_1Nd_2}.
 \tag{VII.2.5}
\]
If two rectangles are centered, the identical scalar and identical
extraction must be used for both. Their original product volumes must be
equal when a later cancellation invokes that equality.

##### 2. Local absolute masses

For a series A write
\[
 \|A\|_{q;s,t}=\sum_{i,j\ge0}|[x^iy^j]A|q^{-si-tj},
 \qquad q=N\mathfrak p.
\]
This positive norm is submultiplicative whenever the displayed sums
converge, by the coefficient convolution and Tonelli's theorem. If
\(s,t\ge\delta\ge0\), (VII.2.1) gives
\[
 \|H-1\|_{q;s,t}\le11q^{-5\delta},\quad
 \|H\|_{q;s,t}\le1+11q^{-5\delta},\quad
 \|B-H\|_{q;s,t}\le14q^{-\delta}.
 \tag{VII.2.6}
\]
The last inequality uses the two degree-one terms and one degree-two term
of B-1, and the eleven terms of H-1.

At s=t=1/2 the quantity \(r=11q^{-5/2}\) is less than 1/2 for q at least 7.
The formal identity \(R=\sum_{k\ge0}(1-H)^k\), whose coefficients are
locally finite because H-1 starts at degree five, is therefore absolutely
summable in this norm. It proves
\[
 \|R\|\le(1-r)^{-1}\le1+2r
 \le1+400q^{-3/2},\qquad
 \|(H-B)R^2\|\le56q^{-1/2}\le10206q^{-1/2}.
 \tag{VII.2.7}
\]
The loose constants on the right match the imported source contracts.
No analytic nonvanishing assertion for a power series is assumed to prove
these estimates.

An extracted marked prime carries its own central normalization. If its
norm is q, include the factor q^{-v}. The three mass regimes needed below
are consequently

| Kernel | (s,t,v) | Unmarked local mass | Marked local mass |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forward | (1/2,1/2,1/2) | 1+11q^{-5/2} | at most 14/q |
| Forward, reflected | (2/3,1/3,2/3) | 1+11q^{-5/3} | at most 14/q |
| Inverse | (1/2,1/2,1/2) | 1+400q^{-3/2} | at most 10206/q |

For an actual annular slot with scale P, coefficient bounded by M and
prime norm q at most 2P, its central coefficient satisfies
\(M/\sqrt P\le\sqrt2M/\sqrt q\le2M/\sqrt q\).
Thus the actual coefficient is bounded by the table times the fixed
product of its slot envelopes. The character phase and natural zero stay
in the exact identity and disappear only in this absolute upper bound.

##### 3. Global masses and common Hilbert norms

The fixed-field ideal count \(\#\{I:NI\le X\}\ll X\) implies
\[
 \sum_{\mathfrak p}(N\mathfrak p)^{-\sigma}<\infty\quad(\sigma>1),
 \qquad \sum_{N\mathfrak p\le X}(N\mathfrak p)^{-1}\ll1+\log(2X).
 \tag{VII.2.8}
\]
The first statement follows by dyadic summation, and the second by the
same argument or partial summation; replacing primes by all ideals is
enough. No prime ideal theorem is needed.

For any of the table's regimes and any fixed distinct marked-prime tuple,
sum the absolute coefficients over an arbitrary finite divisor cutoff.
Enlarge the positive sum to the full Euler product. Its ordinary factors
are bounded by \(\exp(C\sum_{\mathfrak p}(N\mathfrak p)^{-\sigma})\),
and each marked prime contributes at most K/q. Summing over all permitted
distinct marked tuples is bounded by the unrestricted product of the
harmonic sums in (VII.2.8). For a fixed number of marks and prime pools of
polynomial size in Z this is \(O_\epsilon(Z^\epsilon)\). Constants are
chosen after the fixed slot count, envelope and polynomial cap, and before
the actual row character, coefficients, divisor cutoffs and prime sets.
If the slot envelope is variable, its displayed product is retained and
is not hidden in Z^epsilon.

The extraction scalars in (VII.2.5) may depend on the physical row u
through its character and frozen-mark phases. The positive coefficient
masses supply row-independent envelopes w_d>=0 such that
\(|c_d(u)|\le w_d\). For a Hilbert space defined by the original
nonnegative row measure, pointwise multiplication gives
\[
 \|c_d(\cdot)F_d(\cdot)\|\le w_d\|F_d\|,\qquad
 \left\|\sum_d c_d(\cdot)F_d(\cdot)\right\|
 \le\sum_d w_d\|F_d\|.
 \tag{VII.2.9}
\]
This is the triangle inequality applied after retaining the actual
row-dependent phases and zeros. It does not regard them as common complex
scalars or divide by their possibly zero values. The coefficient family,
prime failures, punctures and profiles remain inside each residual row
norm. A mass estimate alone does not establish the residual energy bound.

More precisely, let Q_f be the product of the norms of all frozen marks
in an extracted term, and put
\[
 r_d=\left(\frac{Nd_2}{Nd_1Q_f}\right)^{1/6}.
\]
Multiplying its central weight by r_d changes the two ordinary exponents
from (1/2,1/2) to (2/3,1/3), and each frozen-mark exponent from 1/2 to 2/3.
Thus the first two rows of the table prove
\(\sum_d w_d(1+r_d)\ll_\epsilon Z^\epsilon\).
If the actual residual energies are bounded by \(E(3+r_d^2)\), then
\(\sqrt{3+r_d^2}\le2(1+r_d)\), so (VII.2.9) proves energy at most
\(C_\epsilon Z^\epsilon E\), after choosing half the final epsilon in
the mass estimate before squaring. The whole frozen product Q_f is needed
in this identity. Dropping some frozen factors changes the required mass.

##### 4. Common punctures and collisions of marked primes

At a prime that is to be excluded from both ordinary factors the local
correction to T_4 is
\[
 J=BR=1/T_4,\qquad JT_4=1.
 \tag{VII.2.10}
\]
For s,t at least 1/3 its absolute mass is uniformly bounded. Indeed
z=q^{-1/3} is at most 11/20, and
\[
 \|H-1\|_{q;s,t}\le6z^5+5z^6
 \le28183925/64000000<1/2.
\]
Hence \(\|R\|\le2\), \(\|B\|\le(1+z)^2<3\), and
\(\|J\|\le6\le576\). If all common punctures divide a nonzero ideal F
with \(NF\le Z^{B_0}\), their entire mass is at most
\(576^{\omega(F)}\ll_{\epsilon,B_0} Z^\epsilon\).
For completeness, the divisor estimate here follows by choosing a norm
threshold so that \(576\le q^\eta\) above it; the finitely many smaller
prime ideals contribute a fixed constant. Choose eta after B_0 and epsilon.
When B_0=0, F is the unit ideal and the assertion is immediate.

The same argument covers the central and reflected ordinary weights,
including \((Nd_2/Nd_1)^{1/6}\), for these common puncture kernels.
The remaining live primes must be disjoint from the punctures. This
disjointness is retained in the exact finite expansion, not discarded
after a probability estimate.

To restore repeated marks, partition the fixed r slot indices by equality
of their actual prime values. There are at most \(2^{r^2}\) possible
partitions. For a block J of at least two indices suppose its nonnegative
coefficient envelopes satisfy
\(v_i(p)\le B\), \(\sum_pv_i(p)^2\le L B^2\), with B,L at least one.
Cauchy on two indices and the supremum bound on the others give
\[
 \sum_p\prod_{i\in J}v_i(p)\le L B^{|J|}.
 \tag{VII.2.11}
\]
Freeze each such block at its actual prime. The assignment mass over all
non-singleton blocks is at most \((LB^r)^r\), a convenient loose bound.
Singleton marks retain their phases and are constrained to avoid the
frozen primes and one another. They are precisely the distinct live
family with a common puncture. If every such residual norm is at most
\(\sqrt E\), uniformly in the frozen choices, weighted triangle and
(VII.2.11) bound the full energy by
\[
 [2^{r^2}(LB^r)^r]^2E.
 \tag{VII.2.12}
\]
There is no factor equal to the number of possible prime assignments.
In annular applications L and B are fixed or explicitly paid subpower
envelopes. Any polynomial dependence of these quantities must be charged
before using (VII.2.12).

The puncture and collision bounds are coefficient bounds. All analytic
profile, height and shortened-scale conditions still belong to the
residual source theorem. In particular this section has not replaced a
coupled moment by a product of separate moments.


### C.2. Whole-column fourth-power transfer


Use the supported primary-generator and Gauss conventions of Chapters
1–2. For a supported nonzero modulus a, write chi_a for the sextic
character with its natural nonunit zeros and
\[
 \mathfrak g_a(k)=(Na)^{-1/2}\sum_{x\bmod a}\chi_a(x)e(kx/a).
\]
The unit modulus has Gauss sum one. If a is fifth-free, meaning each of
its prime valuations is at most four, then for every supported ideal D
with its fixed primary generator d_D, and every frequency k,
\[
 \mathfrak g_a(d_D^4k)=\chi_a(d_D)^2\mathfrak g_a(k).
 \tag{VII.3.1}
\]

If D is coprime to a, multiplication by d_D^4 permutes the finite residue
ring. Changing variables gives the multiplier chi_a(d_D)^(-4), equal
to chi_a(d_D)^2 because its sixth power is one at units. If D shares a
prime p with a, let p^j exactly divide a. Then 1<=j<=4 and p^j divides
d_D^4k. In the exact CRT factorization, the additive character in the
local p^j factor is therefore trivial. Its multiplicative character is
the nonprincipal j-th power of the primitive sextic residue character,
lifted from the residue field. The complete local sum vanishes. Its CRT
unit multipliers do not change that divisibility. Thus the left side is
zero. The right side is also zero by chi_a(d_D)=0. This includes k=0.
No character value at a nonunit has been inverted.

Let finitely many supported nonzero columns a_i and coefficients b_i
be given, with every a_i for which b_i is nonzero fifth-free. Put
\[
 P(k)=\sum_i b_i\mathfrak g_{a_i}(k).
\]
The entire coefficient vector is common to all D and k. Summing
(VII.3.1), before taking absolute values, gives
\[
 \sum_i b_i\chi_{a_i}(d_D)^2\mathfrak g_{a_i}(k)=P(d_D^4k).
 \tag{VII.3.2}
\]
This preserves every cross-column phase in one polynomial. It does not
assert that cubic twists disappear after squaring.

Here is the exact positive-family bound. Let D range over a finite set
of supported nonzero ideals with ND<=2W, and k over a finite set of
nonzero elements with Nk<=K, where W,K>0. Suppose
\(0\le w_D\le A\) and \(0\le\rho(D,k)\le1\). For every epsilon>0,
\[
\begin{split}
&\frac1W\sum_Dw_D\sum_k\rho(D,k)
 \left|\sum_i b_i\chi_{a_i}(d_D)^2\mathfrak g_{a_i}(k)\right|^2\\
&\qquad\le
 \frac{C_\epsilon A(16KW^4)^\epsilon}{W}
 \sum_{r\in\{d_D^4k\}}|P(r)|^2.
\end{split}
 \tag{VII.3.3}
\]
To prove it, substitute (VII.3.2) and regroup the nonnegative sum by
r=d_D^4k. Since r is nonzero, D divides the ideal (r). For each ideal D
its primary generator is fixed, so k is uniquely determined. A fiber
therefore has at most tau((r)) members. The elementary ideal-divisor
bound gives tau((r))<=C_epsilon (Nr)^epsilon, and
\(Nr=(ND)^4Nk\le16KW^4\). Its total weight is at most A times this
fiber bound. Sum over r and divide by W. If the indexing family is
empty the inequality is immediate; otherwise Nr>=1 makes the displayed
positive radius meaningful.

The zero frequency was excluded only from the positive pushforward
(VII.3.3), where the divisor-fiber bound requires r!=0. Its exact finite
identity remains (VII.3.1), and its separate source cost is retained in
Appendix C.8. Actual selected-fiber weights and any outside Cauchy cardinality
are also supplied there. This algebraic statement alone supplies no
bound for the residual Gauss energy on the right.

The proof transcribes Sil's PR74 common-column transfer, retained at the
pinned PR76 version. It uses only the previously proved finite local
Gauss, CRT and ideal-divisor facts. Non-fifth-free moduli are not silently
included: they require their complete prime-power defect terms.


### C.3. The sextic sieve and completed reference estimate


Work over the fixed Eisenstein field \(K=\mathbf Q(\omega)\), with \(\mathcal O=\mathbf Z[\omega]\), the primary generators and trace Fourier normalization of Appendix A.1–A.2. Write \(NI\) for the absolute norm of an ideal and \(Nz=|\iota(z)|^2\) for an element.

An ideal is **supported** if it is nonzero and has no prime factor above \(2\) or \(3\). Additional fixed deletions, including the target conductor primes, are permitted by restriction. An ideal is sixth-power-free when every prime valuation lies in \(\{0,\ldots,5\}\).

Put
\[
\chi_I(z)=\prod_{\mathfrak p\mid I}
 \chi_{\mathfrak p}(z)^{v_{\mathfrak p}(I)}.
\]
Every local character power retains its zero at nonunits. In particular,
\[
\chi_I(z)^6=\mathbf1_{(I,(z))=1},
\tag{VII.4.1}
\]
whereas \(\chi_1(z)=1\), including at \(z=0\).

For finite ideal sets \(\mathcal R,\mathcal C\), define
\[
\mathcal E(\mathcal R,\mathcal C;a)
 =\sum_{R\in\mathcal R}
 \left|\sum_{I\in\mathcal C}a_I\chi_I(d_R)\right|^2,
 \qquad
 \|a\|_{\mathcal C}^2=\sum_{I\in\mathcal C}|a_I|^2.
\]
Here \(d_R\) is the prescribed primary generator. The vector \(a\) is common to the entire row family.

**Theorem.** For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(C_\varepsilon>0\), depending only on \(\varepsilon\) and the fixed field and conventions, such that, for \(M,N\ge1\), supported sixth-power-free families satisfying
\[
NR\le M,\qquad NI\le N
\]
obey
\[
\mathcal E(\mathcal R,\mathcal C;a)
 \le C_\varepsilon(MN)^\varepsilon
 \left(M+N+M^{5/6}N^{1/3}+M^{1/3}N^{5/6}\right)
 \|a\|_{\mathcal C}^2.
\tag{VII.4.2}
\]
The constant is chosen before the lengths, families and complex coefficient vector.

The proof below also supplies the completed reference estimate needed when neither ideal index is sixth-power-free.

##### 1. Finite operators, reciprocity and initial control

Let \(\Theta(M,N)\) be the squared operator norm of the matrix
\[
\bigl(\chi_I(d_R)\bigr)_
 {\substack{R\ {\rm supported,\ sixth\!-\!free},\ NR\le M\\
             I\ {\rm supported,\ sixth\!-\!free},\ NI\le N}},
\]
and let \(\Lambda(M,N)\) have the same columns and all supported ideal rows \(NR\le M\).

These are finite matrices. Extending a vector by zero proves monotonicity in both lengths, bounds all prescribed subfamilies, and gives
\[
\Theta(M,N)\le\Lambda(M,N).
\tag{VII.4.3}
\]
If \(0<M<1\), then \(\Lambda(M,N)=0\).

The established reciprocity law, extended multiplicatively with its nonunit zeros, is
\[
\chi_I(d_R)=\epsilon(\operatorname{ray}I,\operatorname{ray}R)
             \chi_R(d_I),\qquad |\epsilon|\le1.
\tag{VII.4.4}
\]
The ray coordinate takes sixteen values. Split the rows into these sixteen classes. On each class, the matrix is a restriction of the transposed reverse matrix followed by a column multiplier of modulus at most one. The triangle inequality for operator norms and invariance under complex transpose therefore give
\[
\Theta(M,N)\le256\,\Theta(N,M).
\tag{VII.4.5}
\]
The same finite-family statement holds without either power-free restriction.

We first prove
\[
\Lambda(M,N)\ll M+N^2 \qquad(M,N\ge1).
\tag{VII.4.6}
\]

Fix a nonnegative compact Schwartz majorant \(W_0\ge1\) on \([0,1]\). For distinct sixth-free columns \(I,J\), write
\[
D=(I,J),\qquad I=DU,\qquad J=DV,\qquad (U,V)=1.
\]
Multiplicativity and (VII.4.1) give the exact identity
\[
\chi_I(z)\overline{\chi_J(z)}
 =\mathbf1_{(D,(z))=1}\chi_U(z)\overline{\chi_V(z)}.
\tag{VII.4.7}
\]
The coprime residual character is nonprincipal: at a prime of \(U\) or \(V\), its local exponent lies between one and five.

Its conductor is \(\operatorname{rad}(UV)\). Primitive Poisson summation from Appendix A.4, equation (47), gives, for every \(A>0\),
\[
\left|\sum_z\chi_U(z)\overline{\chi_V(z)}W_0(Nz/A)\right|
 \ll_{W_0}\sqrt{N\operatorname{rad}U\,N\operatorname{rad}V}.
\]
Indeed, the zero Fourier coefficient vanishes, each normalized primitive Gauss factor has modulus one, and
\[
\sum_{k\ne0}(1+tNk)^{-m}\ll_m t^{-1}\qquad(t>0,\ m>1).
\]
The latter follows directly from the fixed-lattice count \(O(X)\).

Expand the mask in (VII.4.7) over squarefree divisors of \(D\), and rescale the element variable in each term. This costs at most \(2^{\omega(D)}\), uniformly for every resulting positive scale. Since
\[
2^{\omega(D)}\le ND,\qquad
ND\sqrt{N\operatorname{rad}U\,N\operatorname{rad}V}
 \le\sqrt{NI\,NJ}\le N,
\]
the off-diagonal smoothed Gram entry is \(O_{W_0}(N)\). The diagonal entry is \(O_{W_0}(M)\), by lattice counting and \(|\chi_I|\le1\).

There are \(O(N)\) ideal columns. Expanding the square and using
\[
\left(\sum_I|a_I|\right)^2
 \le\#\mathcal C\sum_I|a_I|^2
\]
proves (VII.4.6). This argument permits repeated prime factors in both columns and their gcd.

The only primitive finite-field input used here is elementary. For a nonprincipal multiplicative character \(\theta\),
\[
\left|\sum_x\theta(x)e(x)\right|^2=q.
\]
To verify it, substitute \(x=uy\) in the square: the inner additive sum over \(y\ne0\) is \(q-1\) for \(u=1\), and \(-1\) otherwise; then use \(\sum_u\theta(u)=0\). CRT gives the corresponding product statement, with the nonunit Fourier zeros retained.

##### 2. Sixth-power extraction in the rows

Every supported ideal has a unique decomposition
\[
R=R_0D^6,\qquad R_0\text{ sixth-free},
\]
with no coprimality condition between \(R_0,D\). By (VII.4.1),
\[
\chi_I(d_R)
 =\chi_I(d_{R_0})\mathbf1_{(I,D)=1}.
\tag{VII.4.8}
\]
For fixed \(D\), this replaces \(a_I\) by the common vector
\(a_I\mathbf1_{(I,D)=1}\), whose mass contracts. Consequently,
\[
\Lambda(M,N)
 \le\sum_{\substack{D\ {\rm supported}\\ND\le M^{1/6}}}
       \Theta\!\left(\frac{M}{(ND)^6},N\right).
\tag{VII.4.9}
\]
This is a bound obtained from an exact partition and exact masks; it does not identify the punctured polynomial with the original polynomial.

For \(s>1\), let
\[
Z_{\rm supp}(s)=\sum_{D\ {\rm supported}}(ND)^{-s}<\infty.
\]
Convergence follows by dyadic summation from the fixed-field ideal count. We will repeatedly use
\[
\#\{D:ND\le X\}\ll X.
\tag{VII.4.10}
\]

For \(\alpha\ge7/6\), consider the exponent assertion
\[
\Theta(M,N)\ll_\delta(MN)^\delta
 E_\alpha(M,N),\qquad
E_\alpha(M,N)=M+N^\alpha+M^{5/6}N^{1/3},
\tag{VII.4.11}
\]
for every \(\delta>0\). It implies the completed assertion
\[
\Lambda(L,B)\ll_\delta(LB)^\delta
 \bigl(L^\alpha+L^{1/6}B\bigr),
 \qquad L>0,\ B\ge1.
\tag{VII.4.12}
\]

For \(L<1\), this is immediate. For \(L\ge1\), apply (VII.4.9), reciprocity, and (VII.4.11). Writing \(d=ND\), the three resulting sums are bounded by
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{d\le L^{1/6}} B&\ll L^{1/6}B,\\
\sum_D(L/d^6)^\alpha&\le Z_{\rm supp}(6\alpha)L^\alpha,\\
\sum_D B^{5/6}(L/d^6)^{1/3}
 &\le Z_{\rm supp}(2)L^{1/3}B^{5/6}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Also
\[
L^{1/3}B^{5/6}\le L^\alpha+L^{1/6}B:
\]
if \(B\le L\), it is at most \(L^{7/6}\le L^\alpha\); if \(B\ge L\), it is at most \(L^{1/6}B\). The loss factor in every term is at most \((LB)^\delta\). This proves (VII.4.12), including its complete length range.

The initial estimate proves (VII.4.11) with \(\alpha=2\).

##### 3. Exact primitive-pair Poisson formula

For sixth-free \(I\), put
\[
r=\operatorname{rad}I,\qquad U=I/r.
\]
The primitive character \(\chi_I\) has modulus \(r\): its local exponent at each prime is in \(\{1,\ldots,5\}\). Let \(m_I\) be the product of the prescribed prime generators, so
\[
(m_I)=r,\qquad |m_I|=\sqrt{Nr}.
\]
Let \(\gamma_I\) be its normalized trace Gauss sum; the finite-field calculation above and CRT give \(|\gamma_I|=1\).

For coprime sixth-free \(I,J\), primitive Poisson gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_z\chi_I(z)\overline{\chi_J(z)}W(Nz/M)\\
&\quad=\frac{M\Gamma(I,J)}{\sqrt{Nr\,Nt}}
 \sum_k\overline{\chi_I(k)}\chi_J(k)\,
 \mathscr FW\!\left(\frac{MNk}{Nr\,Nt}\right),
\end{aligned}
\tag{VII.4.13}
\]
where \(t=\operatorname{rad}J\) and \(\mathscr F\) is the manuscript’s radial Fourier transform, not its Mellin transform.

This is precisely equation (47) with primitive modulus \(m_Im_J\) and no extra mask. Its trace character, measure, scale and nonunit zeros coincide with the existing formula. The character exponents are now the actual multiplicities \(e\) and \(6-e\), rather than a fixed cubic specialization.

The exact CRT multiplier is
\[
\Gamma(I,J)
 =\overline{\chi_J(-1)}\,\gamma_I\overline{\gamma_J}\,
       \chi_I(m_J)\overline{\chi_J(m_I)}.
\tag{VII.4.14}
\]
Reflection of a Gauss sum proves the inverse-character factor
\(\gamma(\chi^{-1})=\chi^{-1}(-1)\overline{\gamma(\chi)}\); CRT then proves (VII.4.14).

Write \(m_I=u_Id_r\). Record the finite label
\[
\ell(I)=\bigl(u_I,\ e_I,\ \operatorname{ray}r\bigr),\qquad
e_I=((NI-1)/6)\bmod6.
\]
There are \(6\cdot6\cdot16=576\) labels. If
\(h_e(u)=\iota(u^e)\), set
\[
\eta(\ell(I),\ell(J))
 =\overline{h_{e_J}(-1)}h_{e_I}(u_J)
   \overline{h_{e_J}(u_I)}
   \epsilon(\operatorname{ray}r,\operatorname{ray}t).
\]
Substituting \(m_I=u_Id_r,m_J=u_Jd_t\) in (VII.4.14), and applying reciprocity to the squarefree radicals, gives
\[
\Gamma(I,J)
 =\eta(\ell(I),\ell(J))\gamma_I\overline{\gamma_J}
       \chi_U(d_t)\overline{\chi_V(d_r)},
\qquad |\eta|\le1,
\tag{VII.4.15}
\]
where \(J=tV\). Thus the repeated parts remain coupled.

For a fixed nonzero bad-prime factor \(c\), define
\[
A_I(c)=
 \frac{\overline{a_I\gamma_I\overline{\chi_I(c)}}}{\sqrt{Nr}}.
\]
Then
\[
|A_I(c)|^2\le\frac{|a_I|^2}{Nr}.
\tag{VII.4.16}
\]
For a supported frequency ideal \(K\), the summand obtained from the weighted Gram entry \(a_I\overline{a_J}\) times (VII.4.13), excluding its outside factor \(M\), is exactly
\[
\eta(\ell(I),\ell(J))\,
 \overline{A_I(c)}A_J(c)\,
 \mathcal X(U,V,r,t,K)\,
 \mathscr FW\!\left(\frac{M|c|^2NK}{Nr\,Nt}\right),
\tag{VII.4.17}
\]
where
\[
\mathcal X
 =\chi_U(d_t)\overline{\chi_V(d_r)}
   \overline{\chi_{rU}(d_K)}\chi_{tV}(d_K).
\]
On fixed radical ray classes, reciprocity factors this as
\[
\mathcal X
 =\zeta(U,V;\operatorname{ray}r,\operatorname{ray}t)\,
   \overline{\chi_U(d_K)}\chi_V(d_K)\,
   \overline{\chi_r(d_{KV})}\chi_t(d_{KU}),
\qquad |\zeta|\le1.
\tag{VII.4.18}
\]
Both identities hold with their natural zeros. No division by a character value occurs.
For independent left and right vectors use their corresponding separate coefficient transforms.
After fixing the radical ray classes and finite labels, the factor
\(\zeta(U,V;\operatorname{ray}r,\operatorname{ray}t)
\overline{\chi_U(d_K)}\chi_V(d_K)\) is a bounded multiplier of the common
row \((U,V,K)\). Retain it through the complete inner coprime \((r,t)\)-sum,
then contract it in the row norm. No separation into independent U and V
factors is required or asserted; the block norms below introduce no
repeated-part cardinality factor.

##### 4. The coherent block estimate

We give the finite operator argument used to estimate (VII.4.17).

For nonzero column ideals \(R,T\),
\[
\mathbf1_{(R,T)=1}
 =\sum_{\substack{D\mid R\\D\mid T}}\mu(D).
\]
For arbitrary matrices \(A,B\) with a common row index, expand this identity inside
\[
\sum_x\left|
 \sum_{R,T:(R,T)=1}
   \overline{A_{xR}a_R}B_{xT}b_T\right|.
\]
The triangle inequality followed by Cauchy over \((D,x)\) bounds its square by
\[
\left(\|A\|^2\sum_R\tau(R)|a_R|^2\right)
\left(\|B\|^2\sum_T\tau(T)|b_T|^2\right).
\tag{VII.4.19}
\]
This follows because the projection onto \(D\mid R\) is a column projection, and
\(\sum_D\|a\mathbf1_{D\mid R}\|^2=\sum_R\tau(R)|a_R|^2\).
Thus ideals of norm at most \(X\) cost only \(O_\varepsilon(X^\varepsilon)\).

Retain the repeated parts as block indices:
\[
a=a_{U,r},\qquad b=b_{V,t}.
\]
The left matrix has rows \((V,K)\), columns \(r\), and entry
\(\chi_r(d_{VK})\); the right matrix has rows \((U,K)\), columns \(t\).
Their block extensions have common rows \((U,V,K)\). For example,
\[
\sum_{U,V,K}\left|\sum_r A_{(V,K),r}a_{U,r}\right|^2
 \le\|A\|^2\sum_{U,r}|a_{U,r}|^2.
\]
There is no factor equal to the number of repeated-part indices.

The map \((V,K)\mapsto VK\) has at most \(\tau(Q)\) representations of any nonzero ideal \(Q\). Therefore, if \(N(VK)\le L\) and \(Nr\le B\),
\[
\|A\|^2\ll_\varepsilon L^\varepsilon\Lambda(L,B).
\tag{VII.4.20}
\]
Combining (VII.4.19)–(VII.4.20) proves the required coherent bound. It applies to the common vectors \(a_{U,r}\) and \(b_{V,t}\), without assigning arbitrary coefficients independently to the enlarged rows.

We also need uniform separation of the radial weight. On
\(1\le x,y,z\le2\), write
\[
\mathscr FW(H z/(xy))
 =\int_{\mathbf R}b_H(v)
       e^{iv(-\log x-\log y+\log z)}\,dv,
\]
with the Fourier normalization absorbed into \(v\). For every fixed \(m\),
\[
\int|b_H(v)|\,dv\ll_{W,m}(1+H)^{-m}.
\tag{VII.4.21}
\]
To prove this, choose a fixed smooth cutoff equal to one on the possible interval for \(\log z-\log x-\log y\), and Fourier-transform
\(\vartheta(u)\mathscr FW(He^u)\). Its zeroth and second derivative \(L^1\) norms are \(O_{W,m}((1+H)^{-m})\), by Schwartz decay. Fourier integration by parts gives (VII.4.21). Only finitely many Schwartz seminorms are used.

All separated phases have modulus one and preserve coefficient mass. Finite sums commute with the integral by its absolute \(L^1\) bound. For sums of group norms, align each original group by one scalar of modulus at most one before integrating. The alignment is independent of \(v\); consequently no group-cardinality loss is introduced.

##### 5. Frequency bands and the analytic recurrence

Partition the columns by their 576-valued label and a dyadic radical scale:
\[
P\le Nr\le2P,\qquad Q\le Nt\le2Q.
\]
There are \(O(\log N)\) classes. The repeated parts satisfy
\[
NU\le N/P,\qquad NV\le N/Q.
\]

Every nonzero element frequency has a unique representation
\[
k=c\,d_K,\qquad c=u\lambda^a2^b,\quad K\ {\rm supported}.
\]
For \(X/2\le Nk\le X\), the number of possible bad-prime labels \(c\) is
\(O((1+\log X)^2)\), hence \(O_\varepsilon(X^\varepsilon)\).
Writing \(q=|c|^2\ge1\), its supported ideal frequency satisfies
\[
X/(2q)\le NK\le X/q.
\]
Thus the two enlarged lengths are at most \(NX/Q\) and \(NX/P\).
The Fourier decay scale is exactly
\[
\frac{Mq}{PQ}\frac{X}{2q}=\frac{MX}{2PQ}.
\]
The bad-prime factor cancels from this scale and only shortens the enlarged row ranges; its character factors remain in (VII.4.16)–(VII.4.18).

For a fixed column class, (VII.4.16) contributes the mass factors \(P^{-1}\), \(Q^{-1}\). Define
\[
\mathcal D_\varepsilon(P,L)
 =C_\varepsilon L^\varepsilon\Lambda(L,2P)(2P)^\varepsilon/P.
\]
Equations (VII.4.17)–(VII.4.21) consequently bound the sum of absolute dual-family values over one band by
\[
\ll_\varepsilon
 \frac{X^\varepsilon}{(1+MX/(2PQ))^3}
 \sqrt{\mathcal D_\varepsilon(P,NX/Q)
       \mathcal D_\varepsilon(Q,NX/P)}
 \,\|a\|\,\|b\|.
\tag{VII.4.22}
\]
Here \(a,b\) are independent vectors. Keeping them independent is what bounds the full coprime Gram operator, including complex tests.

Assume, for some \(1\le\alpha\le2\),
\[
\Lambda(L,B)\le A(LB)^\varepsilon
                   (L^\alpha+L^{1/6}B)
\quad(L>0,\ B\ge1).
\tag{VII.4.23}
\]
Put
\[
t=\frac M{2PQ},\quad
U_0=(2N/M)^\alpha N^{\alpha-1},\quad
V_0=2(2N/M)^{1/6}N^{1/6}.
\]
Because \(1\le P,Q\le N\), substitution in either density gives
\[
\sqrt{\mathcal D_\varepsilon(P,NX/Q)
       \mathcal D_\varepsilon(Q,NX/P)}
 \ll_\varepsilon
 A(2N^2X)^{2\varepsilon}
 \bigl(U_0(tX)^\alpha+V_0(tX)^{1/6}\bigr).
\tag{VII.4.24}
\]
For example,
\[
(NX/Q)^\alpha/P
 =(2N/M)^\alpha P^{\alpha-1}(tX)^\alpha
 \le U_0(tX)^\alpha.
\]
The \(1/6\) term follows in the same way. The auxiliary product length is at most \(2N^2X\).

For \(0<\varepsilon<1/6\), both
\(\alpha+3\varepsilon\) and \(1/6+3\varepsilon\) lie in \((0,3)\). For \(0<\nu<3\),
\[
\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{2^{j\nu}}{(1+t2^j)^3}\ll_\nu t^{-\nu}.
\tag{VII.4.25}
\]
If \(t\le1\), split at \(t2^j=1\) and sum the two geometric series; if \(t\ge1\), the whole sum is bounded by \(O_\nu(t^{-3})\le O_\nu(t^{-\nu})\).

Apply (VII.4.25) to (VII.4.22)–(VII.4.24), with \(X=2^j\). A fixed pair of column classes costs
\[
\ll_{\varepsilon,\alpha,W}
 A N^{4\varepsilon}t^{-3\varepsilon}(U_0+V_0)\|a\|\|b\|.
\]
Since \(P,Q\le N\),
\[
N^{4\varepsilon}t^{-3\varepsilon}
 \le2^{3\varepsilon}N^{10\varepsilon}M^{-3\varepsilon}.
\]
The two column-class counts cost at most another \(N^{2\varepsilon}\).
Thus the complete nonzero Poisson series is absolutely summable and costs
\[
\ll A N^{12\varepsilon}M^{-3\varepsilon}
                  (U_0+V_0)\|a\|\|b\|.
\tag{VII.4.26}
\]
At zero frequency, natural zeros leave only \(I=J=1\), contributing at most
\(|\mathscr FW(0)|\|a\|\|b\|\). Restoring the outside factor \(M\) in Poisson, and observing
\[
MU_0=2^\alpha M^{1-\alpha}N^{2\alpha-1},
\qquad
MV_0=2^{7/6}M^{5/6}N^{1/3},
\]
bounds the smoothed coprime Gram operator, for every \(M>0,N\ge1\), by a constant times
\[
\mathcal T(M,N)
 =M+A N^{12\varepsilon}M^{-3\varepsilon}
       \left(M^{1-\alpha}N^{2\alpha-1}
             +M^{5/6}N^{1/3}\right).
\tag{VII.4.27}
\]

It remains to remove the coprime-pair restriction. Sort each original Gram pair by \(D=(I,J)\), use (VII.4.7), expand its mask over \(E\mid D\), and set \(z=d_Ew\). The descendant coefficients are
\[
a^{D,E}_{I/D}
 =\mathbf1_{D\mid I}\,a_I\chi_{I/D}(d_E),
\]
and their lengths are
\[
M'=M/NE,\qquad N'=N/ND,\qquad 1\le NE\le ND\le N.
\]
Their total mass satisfies
\[
\sum_D\sum_{E\mid D}\|a^{D,E}\|^2
 \le\sum_I|a_I|^2\sum_{D\mid I}\tau(D)
 \le\sum_I\tau(I)^2|a_I|^2
 \ll_\varepsilon N^\varepsilon\|a\|^2.
\tag{VII.4.28}
\]
Repeated column primes and all new natural zeros are included in this inequality.

For \(1\le e\le d\),
\[
(M/e)^p(N/d)^q\le M^pN^q
\]
whenever \(q\ge0\) and \(p+q\ge0\). Apply this to
\[
(p,q)=(-3\varepsilon,12\varepsilon),\
(1-\alpha,2\alpha-1),\
(5/6,1/3).
\]
Hence \(\mathcal T(M/e,N/d)\le\mathcal T(M,N)\). The descendant row scale may be below one; (VII.4.27) was proved for every positive scale. Compact positive smoothing and (VII.4.28) now prove the full recurrence
\[
\boxed{\;
\Lambda(M,N)\ll_{\varepsilon,\alpha}
 N^\varepsilon\!
 \left[M+A N^{12\varepsilon}M^{-3\varepsilon}
 \left(M^{1-\alpha}N^{2\alpha-1}
       +M^{5/6}N^{1/3}\right)\right].
\;}
\tag{VII.4.29}
\]
All constants precede \(M,N,A\) and the coefficient families.

##### 6. Exponent improvement and the symmetric majorant

Suppose (VII.4.11) holds for \(7/6<\alpha\le2\). Section 2 supplies (VII.4.23) for every positive loss.

Set
\[
\alpha'=\frac{12\alpha-7}{6\alpha-1},
\qquad
a=\frac{12\alpha-8}{6\alpha-1},
\qquad T=\max(M,N^a).
\]
Then
\[
1\le a\le\alpha',\quad
\frac56a+\frac13=\alpha',\quad
a(1-\alpha)+2\alpha-1=\alpha'.
\]
Since \(1-\alpha<0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
T&\le M+N^{\alpha'},\\
T^{1-\alpha}N^{2\alpha-1}&\le N^{\alpha'},\\
T^{5/6}N^{1/3}
 &\le M^{5/6}N^{1/3}+N^{\alpha'}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the sum of these three terms is at most \(3E_{\alpha'}(M,N)\).

Given a requested loss \(\delta>0\), choose
\[
\varepsilon=\min(\delta/13,1/12).
\]
Use monotonicity \(\Theta(M,N)\le\Lambda(T,N)\), apply (VII.4.29), and use \(T\ge1\). The outside losses are bounded by
\[
N^{13\varepsilon}\le(MN)^\delta.
\]
This proves (VII.4.11) with \(\alpha'\).

Starting at \(\alpha_0=2\), iterate this map. Direct calculation gives
\[
\alpha_{j+1}-\frac76
 =\frac{5(\alpha_j-7/6)}{6\alpha_j-1}
 \le\frac56\left(\alpha_j-\frac76\right).
\]
Consequently \(7/6<\alpha_j\le2\) and
\[
\alpha_j-\frac76\le(5/6)^{j+1}.
\]
For any requested final \(\varepsilon>0\), choose a fixed finite \(j\) with
\(\alpha_j<7/6+\varepsilon/2\), then use (VII.4.11) with loss \(\varepsilon/2\).

If \(N\le M\),
\[
N^{7/6}\le M^{5/6}N^{1/3};
\]
hence the resulting exponent shape is bounded by twice
\((MN)^{\varepsilon/2}\) times the majorant in (VII.4.2).
If \(M<N\), first use reciprocity (VII.4.5) and interchange the lengths.
The majorant is symmetric. This proves (VII.4.2), with a permissible final factor \(512\) in the constant.

The iteration count and all intermediate losses are fixed after the final loss is chosen. No iteration depth or implicit constant depends on the lengths or coefficient vector.

##### 7. Completed rows, element rows and central columns

Define
\[
\mathcal R(M,N)
 =M+M^{1/6}N+M^{5/6}N^{1/3}+M^{1/3}N^{5/6}.
\]
Using (VII.4.9) with the proved symmetric bound gives
\[
\Lambda(M,N)\ll_\varepsilon(MN)^\varepsilon\mathcal R(M,N).
\tag{VII.4.30}
\]
Indeed, its four sums are bounded respectively using
\(Z_{\rm supp}(6)\), the count \(O(M^{1/6})\),
\(Z_{\rm supp}(5)\), and \(Z_{\rm supp}(2)\).

For literal nonzero element rows, write uniquely
\(x=c\,d_K\), where \(c=u\lambda^a2^b\) and \(K\) is supported. Twist the common coefficient by
\[
a_I\longmapsto a_I\chi_I(c).
\]
Its mass contracts. There are \(O((1+\log M)^2)\) bad-prime labels for \(Nx\le M\); absorb them using half the requested loss. Apply (VII.4.30) to each supported ideal family.

At \(x=0\), \(\chi_I(0)=\mathbf1_{I=1}\); this row contributes at most \(\|a\|^2\), already dominated by the reference majorant. Therefore
\[
\sum_{\substack{x\in\mathcal X\\Nx\le M}}
 \left|\sum_{I\in\mathcal C}a_I\chi_I(x)\right|^2
 \ll_\varepsilon(MN)^\varepsilon\mathcal R(M,N)\|a\|^2
\tag{VII.4.31}
\]
for arbitrary finite element rows and supported sixth-free columns.

Now remove the column restriction under the literal central hypothesis
\[
|a_I|^2\le A/(NI),\qquad NI\le N.
\tag{VII.4.32}
\]
Write uniquely \(I=JD^6\), with \(J\) sixth-free; overlap between \(J,D\) is allowed. For each \(D\),
\[
F_D(x)=\sum_{I:\,\text{sixth quotient }D}a_I\chi_I(x)
 =\mathbf1_{(D,(x))=1}
     \sum_Ja_{JD^6}\chi_J(x).
\tag{VII.4.33}
\]
For \(\delta>0\), the reduced vector has mass at most
\[
\sum_J|a_{JD^6}|^2
 \le\frac A{(ND)^6}\sum_{NJ\le N}(NJ)^{-1}
 \le\frac{A N^\delta Z_{\rm supp}(1+\delta)}{(ND)^6}.
\tag{VII.4.34}
\]
The mask in (VII.4.33) contracts each fiber energy, so (VII.4.31) applies to that fiber.

Weighted Cauchy gives
\[
\left|\sum_DF_D(x)\right|^2
 \le Z_{\rm supp}(2)\sum_D(ND)^2|F_D(x)|^2.
\]
After summing the fiber energies, the remaining root sum is
\(Z_{\rm supp}(4)\). Choose the reference loss and \(\delta\) each equal to half the requested loss. Since \(N^\delta\le(MN)^\delta\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{\;
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}
 \left|\sum_{I\in\mathcal C}a_I\chi_I(x)\right|^2
 \ll_\varepsilon(MN)^\varepsilon\mathcal R(M,N)\,A.
\;}
\tag{VII.4.35}
\]
Both power-free restrictions are gone. The hypothesis replacing the column restriction is exactly (VII.4.32), not an arbitrary-coefficient assertion.

All displayed reference applications assume \(M,N\ge1\). If a shortened column bound is below one, the ideal column family is empty. If a literal element row bound is below one, only \(x=0\) remains, and (VII.4.32) bounds its energy by \(A\). Thus subunit shortenings have an explicit terminal treatment.

##### 8. The actual common tuple convolution

Let \(S\) be any finite, row-independent set of \(d\)-tuples of ideals, with arbitrary fixed collisions, overlaps and tuple restrictions. Put
\[
I(v)=\prod_{j=1}^dv_j,\qquad
a_I=\sum_{\substack{v\in S\\I(v)=I}}\beta_v.
\]
Then, exactly,
\[
\sum_{v\in S}\beta_v\chi_{I(v)}(x)=\sum_Ia_I\chi_I(x).
\tag{VII.4.36}
\]
Every factor of a tuple with product \(I\) divides \(I\); hence its fiber has at most \(\tau(I)^d\) members. Suppose
\[
I(v)\text{ supported},\quad NI(v)\le N,\quad
|\beta_v|\le B/\sqrt{NI(v)}.
\]
The fixed-field divisor bound, with an arbitrarily small exponent chosen after \(d\), gives
\[
|a_I|^2\ll_{\delta,d}N^\delta B^2/(NI).
\]
Apply (VII.4.35) with half the final loss and absorb this envelope with the other half:
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}
 \left|\sum_{v\in S}\beta_v\chi_{I(v)}(x)\right|^2
 \ll_{\varepsilon,d}(MN)^\varepsilon
          \mathcal R(M,N)B^2.
\tag{VII.4.37}
\]

For the reflected source scales assume
\(Z\ge1, R\ge0, L>0, N\ge1, T\ge0, B\ge0\), and
\(Nx\le Z^R\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\). Suppose
\[
M=Z^R,\quad N\le Z^v,\quad N\le Z^yT,\quad
v\le4R/5,\quad y\le R/2,\quad R+v\le L.
\]
Then
\[
\mathcal R(Z^R,N)\le Z^R(3+T^{1/3}).
\]
The terms \(M^{1/6}N\) and \(M^{1/3}N^{5/6}\) are at most \(Z^R\); the remaining mixed term is at most \(Z^RT^{1/3}\).
Using loss \(\varepsilon/L\) in (VII.4.37) yields
\[
\sum_x\left|\sum_{v\in S}\beta_v\chi_{I(v)}(x)\right|^2
 \ll_{\varepsilon,L,d}Z^{R+\varepsilon}
                (3+T^{1/3})B^2.
\tag{VII.4.38}
\]
Its square-root cost is bounded by
\[
\ll Z^{(R+\varepsilon)/2}(2+T^{1/6})B.
\]

Arbitrary fixed target twists, norm phases and angular factors may enter the common vector without changing these bounds when their modulus is at most one. Common joint profiles are handled by the already established Fourier–Minkowski adapter, provided its finite weighted \(L^1\) envelope is supplied. Independent heights remain independent throughout. A row-dependent coefficient family, or a new angular reflection identity, requires its own adapter and is not asserted by (VII.4.37).


### C.4. Actual selected short-reference estimate


This section completes the passage from Appendix C.3’s common-column sieve to the selected reference used in (5.42), (5.47), and the short-root cases. It uses Appendix C.1, for the already written forward-restoration and common-puncture masses. It does not require another physical source estimate.

Write \(m_0=\mathrm{fixedBadMask}\), and put
\[
C_{\mathrm{pres}}
 =N(m_0)\,N(72),\qquad
R=\log_Z\!\bigl(C_{\mathrm{pres}}N\mathfrak q_\eta K\bigr).
\tag{A.1}
\]
Here \(N(m_0)\) denotes the norm of its principal ideal. The fixed presentation factor is retained in \(R\).

For the selected supplier \(q\), let
\[
V_q=\mathrm{volume}(q),\qquad W_q=\mathrm{scale}(q),\qquad
d=\log_ZV_q.
\]
These are the original and padded selected volumes, respectively. In particular,
\[
W_q=2^{|J_q|}V_q,\qquad |J_q|\le N,
\tag{A.2}
\]
and every actual selected product satisfies
\[
NF\le W_q\le2^NZ^d.
\tag{A.3}
\]
We use \(W_q\), not \(V_q\), in the normalized grouped sum below.

For the source’s displayed ordinary lengths, put
\[
P=\log_Z(X_1X_2).
\]
Let \(S\ge0\) bound its unpadded live marked product:
\[
\prod_{i\in T}P_i\le Z^S.
\]
Assume
\[
P+2S+4d\le R-\rho,\qquad
P+S>\frac56R-\frac73d,\qquad \rho>0.
\tag{A.4}
\]
Define the physical midpoint
\[
\ell_-=\frac32\left(P+S+\frac73d-\frac56R\right),\quad
\ell_+=\frac{P-S-R/2-d}{2},\quad
\ell=\frac{\ell_-+\ell_+}{2}.
\tag{A.5}
\]
The selected short-reference case is
\[
X_1\le Z^\ell\quad\text{or}\quad X_2\le Z^\ell.
\tag{A.6}
\]

The source \(s\) retains its original prime pools, fifth-free ordinary-product restriction, distinct live marks, ordinary and marked holes, ordinary puncture \(R_s\), two original Schwartz profiles \(W_1,W_2\), marked profiles, frequencies and prefixes. Its marked coefficient is the literal canonical coefficient
\[
b_i^t(I)=
 \mathrm{slotCoefficient}(\nu,R_{0},t_0+t;i,I)\,
 W_{\mathrm{slot},i}(NI/P_i).
\tag{A.7}
\]
In particular the shift is \(t_0+t\). Assume its envelopes satisfy \(M_i\le B_f\), where \(B_f\ge1\).

The explicit polynomial caps required below are
\[
\begin{gathered}
R\le B_R,\quad 1\le V_q\le Z^{B_d},\quad W_q\le Z^{B_{\rm sel}},\\
N(F_{\rm hole}R_s)\le Z^{K_{\rm cap}},\qquad
N\mathfrak p\le Z^{K_{\rm cap}}\quad(\mathfrak p\in\mathcal S_s),\\
\prod_i2P_i\le Z^L,\qquad
bX_j\prod_i2P_i\le Z^L\quad(j=1,2),
\end{gathered}
\tag{A.8}
\]
where
\[
L=2(B_R+1),\qquad K_{\rm cap}=B_R+B_d+\rho+1.
\tag{A.9}
\]
The source’s finite enclosing prime set must contain every prime of every supported ordinary ideal with norm at most \(bX_1\) or \(bX_2\). The source hypotheses also retain
\[
\mathfrak p\in\mathcal H_s
 \ \Longrightarrow\ 
 \mathfrak p\mid F_{\rm hole},\quad
 \mathfrak p\in R_{0,i}\quad\text{for every live }i.
\tag{A.10}
\]

For a selected \(F\), let \(\chi_{F,z}\) be the actual `selectedCharacterAt` construction. The retained row predicate may depend on \(F\), but must imply
\[
z\ne0,\qquad
\neg\mathrm{FixedInducingRow}
  \bigl(\eta,Q,m_0,d_F^2,z\bigr),
\quad d_F=\mathrm{primaryGenerator}(F).
\tag{A.11}
\]

**Theorem.** Fix the ambient finite slot type, its bound \(N\), the constants in (A.8)–(A.9), \(a>0,b\ge0,B_f\ge1\), and \(\varepsilon>0\). There are a finite Schwartz control set \(\mathcal C\), containing \((0,0)\), an integer \(J\), a positive constant \(C\), and a threshold for \(Z\), chosen before the source, supplier, characters, profiles, heights and selected products, such that
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{F\in\mathrm{selectedProducts}(q)}
 \frac{g_q(F)}{W_q}\,
 \mathcal E_{\mathrm{keep}_F}
 \left[
   \mathrm{heightRectangle}
       (s,\chi_{F,\bullet},t;X_1,X_2);
       \Phi,K
 \right]\\
&\qquad\le
 \mathrm{radialControl}(\Phi)\,
 C K_{\rm slot}^{2N}
 [\mathcal S_{\mathcal C}(W_1)
  \mathcal S_{\mathcal C}(W_2)]^2
 \mathcal H^J\,N\mathfrak q_\eta K\,Z^\varepsilon,
\end{aligned}
\tag{A.12}
\]
where
\[
\mathcal H=1+|t|+V+|t_1|+|t_2|,\qquad V\ge0,
\]
and \(\operatorname{supp}\Phi\subset(-\infty,2]\).

The weights \(g_q(F)\) are the actual grouped weights
\[
g_q(F)=
 \sum_{\substack{y\in\mathrm{supportedSelected}(q)\\
                  \mathrm{selectedProduct}(q,y)=F}}
       |\mathrm{selectedWeight}(q,y)|^2.
\tag{A.13}
\]
The supplier assumptions are \(|q.\nu_i(I)|\le1\), \(|q.W_{\mathrm{slot},i}|\le K_{\rm slot}\), \(K_{\rm slot}\ge1\), and at most \(N\) slots. No replacement coefficient sequence occurs in (A.12).

Here the radial energy uses \(\Re\Phi\), exactly as in the source definition. Positivity of \(\Phi\) is unnecessary for this upper bound.

##### 1. A common product estimate from Appendix C.3

Suppose a finite character family \(\chi_z\), on element rows \(Nz\le Z^R\), satisfies
\[
a_{\chi_z}(I)=c(I)\chi_I(z)
 \quad(I\text{ supported}),\qquad
a_{\chi_z}(I)=0\quad(I\text{ unsupported}),
\tag{A.14}
\]
where \(c\) is common and \(|c(I)|\le1\).

A finite factor of length \(H\) and amplitude \(B\) means
\[
F(\chi)=\sum_{I\in\mathcal P}a_Ia_\chi(I),\qquad
NI\le H,\qquad |a_I|\le B/\sqrt{NI}.
\]
Multiplying finitely many such factors, grouping by their complete product, and using Appendix C.3’s convolution estimate gives
\[
\sum_z\left|\prod_iF_i(\chi_z)\right|^2
 \ll Z^{R+\epsilon}
       (3+T^{1/3})\left(\prod_iB_i\right)^2
\tag{A.15}
\]
provided the complete product length \(N_c\) satisfies
\[
N_c\le Z^v,\qquad N_c\le Z^yT,\qquad
R+v\le L,\quad v\le4R/5,\quad y\le R/2.
\tag{A.16}
\]
Unsupported coefficients vanish before grouping; the fixed coefficient \(c\) is then absorbed into the common vector.

For a smooth Hecke factor
\[
P_\chi(W,X,u)
 =X^{-1/2}\sum_IW(NI/X)(NI/X)^{2\pi iu}a_\chi(I),
\]
support in \((-\infty,b]\) and \(|W|\le B\) give length \(bX\) and amplitude \(\sqrt b\,B\), since
\[
X^{-1/2}|W(NI/X)|\le\sqrt b\,B/\sqrt{NI}.
\tag{A.17}
\]
Its frequency has modulus one and is retained exactly.

Thus (A.15) applies to two smooth factors and any fixed number of finite marked factors, uniformly in all their common frequencies.

##### 2. Direct or reflected selection of the longer factor

Assume temporarily that every \(\chi_z\) is nonprincipal and its presented modulus has norm at most a common \(U\), with
\[
1\le U\le Z^{K_{\rm cap}}.
\]
For \(A=Z^{\xi/2}\), define
\[
\mathcal B(X,U)=
 \begin{cases}
 bX,&X\le\sqrt U,\\
 4A\,U/X,&X>\sqrt U.
 \end{cases}
\tag{A.18}
\]
Both bounds
\[
\mathcal B(X,U)\le(b+4)A\sqrt U,\qquad
\mathcal B(X,U)\le(b+4)A\,U/X
\tag{A.19}
\]
hold for the **same** selected branch.

The direct branch is (A.17). For completeness, the reflected branch uses the existing natural reflection of Appendix A.5, equation (71), retaining the original character’s redundant zeros. Choose its primitive inducing character \(\psi_z\). If \(\mathcal R_z\) is the redundant natural radical, its exact dual scales have the form
\[
Y_{D,H}
 =\frac{N\mathfrak q_{\psi_z}\,N\prod_{\mathfrak p\in D}\mathfrak p}
        {X\,NH},
\quad D\subseteq\mathcal R_z,\quad
H\text{ supported on }\mathcal R_z,
\tag{A.20}
\]
with
\[
N\mathfrak q_{\psi_z}\,N\mathcal R_z
 \le N\mathfrak q_{\chi_z}\le U.
\]
Consequently \(0<Y_{D,H}\le U/X\). The coefficients are the original deletion/restoration coefficients; their absolute mass is \(O_\delta((N\mathfrak q_{\chi_z})^\delta)\).

After retaining the annuli prescribed by the cutoff \(A\), every nonempty retained annular scale \(Y'\) obeys
\[
1\le Y'\le4A\,U/X.
\tag{A.21}
\]
If this upper bound is below one, the retained family is empty. It is not replaced by a length-one family.

Here is why the common energy (A.15) controls these row-dependent reflected scales. On an annulus, Fourier inversion in logarithmic coordinates separates the transformed profile into common norm-frequency phases. Its Fourier envelope, including finitely many derivatives, is bounded by
\[
C\,\mathcal S_{\mathcal C}(W_{\rm long})
       (1+|t_{\rm long}|)^n
\]
times a fixed integrable decaying function. Apply Minkowski before integrating. Sobolev on the logarithmic scale interval
\([0,\log Y]\), using a function and its first derivative, costs \(1+2\log Y\) in squared energy. The two required tests are precisely the manuscript’s `scaleTest` \(j=0,1\). Gauge away the unit normalization phase before taking a logarithmic scale derivative, so no short-frequency loss is introduced. The common-frequency energies required by this argument are (A.15).

Conjugating the reflected factor inside its absolute value restores the original character orientation and conjugates its profile. This leaves the other factors’ moduli unchanged. The argument therefore applies with an arbitrary fixed physical multiplier, including the product of the other finite factors.

The redundant coefficient mass and the logarithmic scale supremum cost arbitrarily small powers of \(Z\). Polynomial conductor caps make this uniform over all presented characters. All profile controls are finite seminorms chosen before the profiles; the zero profile follows by homogeneity, without division by a seminorm.

Finally, the discarded natural-reflection tail is
\[
\ll C\,\mathcal S_{\mathcal C}(W_{\rm long})
 (1+|t_{\rm long}|)^n Z^{-A_0}
\tag{A.22}
\]
for any fixed \(A_0\), provided
\(N\mathfrak q_{\chi_z}\le Z^{L_{\rm tail}}X\).
In the reflected branch \(X>\sqrt U\ge1\), so the coarse modulus bound supplies this with \(L_{\rm tail}=K_{\rm cap}\). Taking \(A_0=L+1\) pays the remaining factors’ crude \(O(Z^L)\) norm and the \(O(Z^R)\) element-row count.

Equations (A.20)–(A.22) are the original natural reflection, redundant Euler restoration, annular truncation and profile/Sobolev argument of Appendix A.1.3 and A.5.3. The new energy supplied to that argument is (A.15); no old moment estimate is transferred.

We have proved the following selection rule: the product of a long ordinary factor, a short ordinary factor and finite live factors obeys (A.15) when its complete selected length is computed using \(\mathcal B\). The resulting bound has the form
\[
C\,\mathcal S_{\mathcal C}(W_{\rm long})^2
 (1+\mathrm{Height})^{2n}
 Z^{R+\epsilon}(3+T^{1/3})
 \left(\sqrt b\,B_{\rm short}\prod_iB_i\right)^2.
\tag{A.23}
\]

All scales in this argument are positive. A direct factor with empty ideal support is zero. A reflected range below one has no retained annuli, and only its paid tail remains.

##### 3. Apply the forward identity to the actual restricted rectangle

First orient \(X_1\) as the short scale. Put
\[
V_s=\prod_{i\in T}2P_i.
\]

Use Appendix C.1’s exact forward identity, including its nilpotent marked variables, before taking any norm. Partition the live slot labels by the subset \(T_0\) whose marked occurrence supplies a forward correction. Its actual frozen assignment is an injective map
\[
\tau:T_0\longrightarrow\mathcal S_s,\qquad
\tau(i)\in\mathcal P_i.
\]
Write
\[
Q_\tau=\prod_{i\in T_0}N\tau(i).
\]
For each extracted ordinary pair \(e=(e_1,e_2)\), the ordinary scales are exactly
\[
X_1/Ne_1,\qquad X_2/Ne_2.
\tag{A.24}
\]
Both are positive; neither is rounded up.

The remaining marked assignments retain their mutual injectivity and avoid every frozen prime. Group their actual products into one finite factor \(H_{T_0,\tau}\). This factor is formed before the physical character is supplied. Its length satisfies
\[
\operatorname{length}(H_{T_0,\tau})
 =\prod_{i\notin T_0}2P_i
 \le V_s/Q_\tau.
\tag{A.25}
\]
For any \(\delta_a>0\), its amplitude is bounded by
\[
C_{\delta_a,N}
  (\max(1,V_s))^{\delta_a}
  (\sqrt2 B_f)^N.
\tag{A.26}
\]
To prove (A.26), group the remaining tuple coefficients by their whole ideal product. A product \(I\) has at most \(\tau(I)^N\) ordered factorizations; apply the ideal-divisor estimate after the fixed \(N\). All frozen-prime holes and live collision restrictions remain in the tuple set.

The exact rectangle is consequently a finite sum
\[
\sum_{T_0}\sum_{\tau}\sum_e
 c_{\tau,e}(\chi_z)\,
 P_{\chi_z}(W_2,X_2/Ne_2,u_2)
 P_{\chi_z}(W_1,X_1/Ne_1,u_1)
 H_{T_0,\tau}(\chi_z).
\tag{A.27}
\]
The scalar is the actual forward kernel coefficient times
\[
\frac{a_{\chi_z}(e_1e_2)}{\sqrt{Ne_1Ne_2}}
 \prod_{i\in T_0}
 \frac{b_i^t(\tau(i))a_{\chi_z}(\tau(i))}{\sqrt{P_i}}.
\]
Thus every frequency, character phase and natural zero is retained.

By (A.19), (A.24)–(A.25), the same selected child length \(N_c\) satisfies
\[
N_c\le(b+4)A\,bX_1V_s\sqrt U,
\tag{A.28}
\]
and
\[
N_c\le
 (b+4)A\,b\frac{X_1V_sU}{X_2}
 \frac{Ne_2}{Ne_1Q_\tau}.
\tag{A.29}
\]
The denominator in (A.29) contains the entire frozen product \(Q_\tau\).

Suppose the right sides without the final ratio are bounded respectively by \(Z^v,Z^y\). Then (A.23) bounds the child energy by
\[
E\left(3+
 \left(\frac{Ne_2}{Ne_1Q_\tau}\right)^{1/3}\right).
\tag{A.30}
\]
Appendix C.1, §§2–3, gives a common scalar majorant \(w_{\tau,e}\), independent of \(z\), with
\[
|c_{\tau,e}(\chi_z)|\le w_{\tau,e},\qquad
\sum_{\tau,e}w_{\tau,e}
 \left[1+
 \left(\frac{Ne_2}{Ne_1Q_\tau}\right)^{1/6}\right]
 \ll_\delta Z^\delta.
\tag{A.31}
\]
Its central and critical regimes are exactly
\[
(1/2,1/2;1/2),\qquad(2/3,1/3;2/3).
\]
Weighted triangle in the common row Hilbert space, followed by
\(\sqrt{3+r^2}\le2(1+r)\), combines (A.30)–(A.31). It does not cost the number of frozen assignments or extraction pairs.

There are finitely many \(T_0\), at most \(2^N\). Take the union of their finite profile controls, the sum of their height degrees, and a common constant before choosing any profiles.

For explicit loss accounting, let e>0 be the requested restricted-rectangle
loss. Apply (A.23) with loss e/4. Choose the norm-mass exponent in (A.31)
as e/8; its square costs e/4. Choose the tuple-divisor exponent
\(\delta_a=e/(4L)\); since \(V_s\le Z^L\), squaring (A.26) costs e/2.
These three energy losses total e. The remaining finite subset count is
part of the constant. This proves the complete forward restricted bound
with loss e before the separate puncture allocation in the next paragraph.

##### 4. The whole ordinary puncture remains in the coefficients

The source’s puncture \(R_s\) is handled exactly, without changing the row character. Enlarge the common ordinary holes by the primes of \(R_s\), and replace
\[
R_{0,i}\longmapsto R_{0,i}\cup\operatorname{primeSupport}(R_s).
\tag{A.32}
\]
This is a pointwise identity for the canonical marked coefficient and the ordinary coprimality restriction. The new holes divide \(F_{\rm hole}R_s\), whose norm is bounded in (A.8). The new marked coefficients still have envelope \(B_f\), because (A.32) only adds zeros.

At a common hole, apply Appendix C.1’s exact correction \(J=B/H\). Its extracted child has the same shortened scales (A.24), and its reference ratio is \(Ne_2/Ne_1\). Appendix C.1, §4, supplies the common positive mass for both the central and critical weights:
\[
\sum_e w_e
 \left[1+(Ne_2/Ne_1)^{1/6}\right]\ll_\delta Z^\delta.
\tag{A.33}
\]
Apply the preceding restricted estimate with half the requested loss, then spend the other half on (A.33).

This proves the actual short-rectangle estimate once
\[
\begin{gathered}
v=\ell+(R+d_{\rm ref})/2+S+2\delta_{\rm ref},\\
y=R+d_{\rm ref}+2\ell-P+S+2\delta_{\rm ref}
\end{gathered}
\tag{A.34}
\]
satisfy \(R+v\le L,\ v\le4R/5,\ y\le R/2\), and
\[
U\le Z^{R+d_{\rm ref}},\quad
(b+4)b\,2^{|T|}\le Z^{\delta_{\rm ref}},\quad
\xi/2\le\delta_{\rm ref}.
\tag{A.35}
\]
Indeed, \(X_1X_2=Z^P\), \(X_1\le Z^\ell\), and
\(V_s\le2^{|T|}Z^S\) turn (A.28)–(A.29) into (A.34).

The puncture \(F_{\rm hole}R_s\) has entered only (A.32)–(A.33). It has not been inserted into the presented character’s conductor.

##### 5. Construct the actual character and its conductor cap

For each supported selected product \(F\), construct first a sextic row character \(\psi_F\) representing \(I\mapsto\chi_I(d_F)\), with presented modulus norm at most
\[
C_{\rm cub}NF.
\]
Squaring this character preserves its presented modulus and gives
\[
a_{\psi_F^2}(I)=\chi_I(d_F)^2
\]
on supported ideals, with the same nonunit zeros. This is the linear-in-\(NF\) cubic construction. Constructing instead a new sextic character with parameter \(d_F^2\) would give an unnecessarily larger bound and is not the construction used here.

Apply the established row-character construction to
\(\eta\psi_F^2\), the original mask \(m_0\), and \(z\ne0\). It produces the actual \(\chi_{F,z}\) with
\[
a_{\chi_{F,z}}(I)
 =a_\eta(I)\chi_I(d_F)^2\chi_I(m_0^6)\chi_I(z)
 \quad(I\text{ supported}),
\tag{A.36}
\]
zero on unsupported ideals, and
\[
N\mathfrak q_{\chi_{F,z}}
 \le C_{\rm cub}N\mathfrak q_\eta N(m_0)N(72)\,NF\,Nz.
\tag{A.37}
\]
The fixed multiplier in (A.36) has modulus at most one and is common in \(z\), so it is exactly the coefficient identification (A.14).

The construction also gives, on every element \(n\),
\[
a_{\chi_{F,z}}((n))
 =\mathrm{rowTwist}(\eta,m_0,1,d_F^2z;n),
\tag{A.38}
\]
with the original unsupported-element zeros. If this character were principal, it would be induced by the primitive unit character. Since \(Q\le(1)\), (A.38) would witness
\(\mathrm{FixedInducingRow}(\eta,Q,m_0,d_F^2,z)\).
Thus (A.11) proves that the **actual** presented character is nonprincipal. No untwisted \(z\)-predicate is substituted.

On the radial support \(Nz\le2K\), set
\[
U_F=\max\!\left(1,\,
 C_{\rm cub}N\mathfrak q_\eta N(m_0)N(72)\,NF\,(2K)\right).
\tag{A.39}
\]
This is `actualConductorCap`, and (A.37) gives the required modulus cap.

Now choose
\[
\omega=\rho/100,\qquad
d_{\rm ref}=d+\omega,\qquad
\delta_{\rm ref}=\rho/200=\omega/2,\qquad \xi=\omega.
\tag{A.40}
\]
The physical selected exponent remains \(d\); only the reference call uses \(d_{\rm ref}\).

By (A.1), (A.3),
\[
C_{\rm cub}N\mathfrak q_\eta N(m_0)N(72)\,NF\,(2K)
 \le2C_{\rm cub}2^N Z^{R+d}.
\]
A single threshold, independent of all future characters and suppliers, ensures
\(2C_{\rm cub}2^N\le Z^\omega\). Consequently
\[
1\le U_F\le Z^{R+d_{\rm ref}}\le Z^{K_{\rm cap}}.
\tag{A.41}
\]
Also \(N(72)=5184\), so \(C_{\rm pres}\ge2\) and \(N\mathfrak q_\eta\ge1\) give
\[
2K\le C_{\rm pres}N\mathfrak q_\eta K=Z^R.
\tag{A.42}
\]
A second common threshold ensures
\((b+4)b2^N\le Z^{\delta_{\rm ref}}\).
This proves every requirement in (A.35).

##### 6. Verify the reference gates with their reserve

The interval width in (A.5) is
\[
\ell_+-\ell_-=R-P-2S-4d\ge\rho.
\]
Therefore \(0<\ell<P/2\). The midpoint can also be written
\[
\ell=P+\frac S2+\frac{3d}2-\frac{3R}4.
\]
Substituting (A.40) into (A.34) gives
\[
v=P+\frac32S+2d-\frac R4+\frac32\omega,
\qquad
y=P+2S+4d-\frac R2+2\omega.
\]
Using (A.4),
\[
v\le\frac34R-\rho-\frac S2-2d+\frac32\omega
 \le\frac45R,
\]
and
\[
y\le\frac R2-\rho+2\omega\le R/2.
\tag{A.43}
\]
The same hypotheses give \(R>0\); the unsimplified expressions in (A.34) show \(v,y\ge0\). Finally,
\[
R+v\le\frac95R\le L.
\]
The strengthened mixed gate also survives:
\[
P+2S+4d_{\rm ref}
 \le R-\rho+4\omega<R.
\tag{A.44}
\]
This verifies the gates of §4 from the original reserve, rather than assuming them for \(d+\omega\).

##### 7. Original profiles, independent heights and orientation

The exact canonical identity for the row under consideration is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{heightRectangle}
 (s,\chi,t;X_1,X_2)
={}&\mathrm{residualPhase}(s.X_1s.X_2,s.d,1,t)\\
&\times\mathrm{rectangleRow}\!
 \left(\chi;\,
 b_i^t,\,
 \mathrm{phaseProfile}(W_1,u_1),\,
 \mathrm{phaseProfile}(W_2,u_2);
 X_1,X_2\right),
\end{aligned}
\tag{A.45}
\]
where
\[
u_j=(t_j+t)/(2\pi).
\]
The residual phase has modulus one and continues to use the original stored source scales and prefixes. They are not replaced by the displayed reference lengths.

For nonzero pool ideals,
\[
|b_i^t(I)|=|b_i^0(I)|\le M_i\le B_f.
\tag{A.46}
\]
This identity includes every canonical fixed-hole zero.

Let \(H_{\rm ref}=|t|+|t_1|+|t_2|\). Then
\[
|u_j|\le H_{\rm ref},\qquad
1+H_{\rm ref}\le\mathcal H.
\]
Choose a finite Schwartz control set that dominates the long-profile controls from §§2–4 and both short scale tests. Continuity of \(W\mapsto W\), \(W\mapsto xW'\), and the corresponding fixed scale-test combinations gives
\[
\sup_{j=0,1;\,x}|\mathrm{scaleTest}(W_1,j,x)|
 \le D\mathcal S_{\mathcal C}(W_1).
\]
Thus the left-short estimate is homogeneous:
\[
C[\mathcal S_{\mathcal C}(W_1)
  \mathcal S_{\mathcal C}(W_2)]^2\mathcal H^JZ^{R+\epsilon}.
\tag{A.47}
\]
The controls and degree are chosen before both profiles. The zero-profile case requires no normalization.

If \(X_2\) is short, exchange only the two ordinary summation variables, displayed lengths, profiles and their frequencies. The finite rectangle restrictions are symmetric in the two ordinary variables. The marked slots, original source scales, prefixes, punctures, character and residual phase are fixed. This gives exactly the same rectangle and the same estimate (A.47).

To make this uniform over all live \(T\subseteq\iota\), take the finite union of their controls, the sum of their nonnegative height degrees, and \(1+\sum_T C_T\). This occurs before any source or profile is supplied.

##### 8. Radial energy and the actual grouped weights

For fixed \(F\), retain exactly the finite row set
\[
\mathcal Z_F=\{z:\ z\ne0,\ Nz\le2K,\ \mathrm{keep}_F(z)\}.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{supp}\Phi\subset(-\infty,2]\), every other radial summand is zero. Moreover
\[
\Re\Phi(x)\le\sup_y|\Phi(y)|
 =\mathrm{radialControl}(\Phi).
\]
Apply (A.47) on \(\mathcal Z_F\), then (A.1):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal E_{\mathrm{keep}_F}
 [\mathrm{heightRectangle};\Phi,K]
\le{}&
\mathrm{radialControl}(\Phi)\,
 C[\mathcal S_{\mathcal C}(W_1)
   \mathcal S_{\mathcal C}(W_2)]^2
 \mathcal H^J\\
&\times C_{\rm pres}N\mathfrak q_\eta K\,Z^\epsilon.
\end{aligned}
\tag{A.48}
\]
Absorb the fixed \(C_{\rm pres}\) into \(C\). The row keep has remained literal and \(F\)-dependent throughout.

For the weighted result, apply (A.48) with loss \(\varepsilon/2\). Set
\[
\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{2(B_{\rm sel}+1)}.
\tag{A.49}
\]
Every selected assignment in a fiber of product \(F\) has its components among the divisors of \(F\). Since there are at most \(N\) components,
\[
|\mathrm{selectedFiber}(q,F)|
 \le\tau(F)^{|J_q|}
 \ll_{\delta,N}(NF)^\delta.
\]
Each squared selected amplitude is at most \(K_{\rm slot}^{2N}\). Consequently
\[
g_q(F)\ll_{\delta,N}K_{\rm slot}^{2N}(NF)^\delta
 \ll_{\delta,N}K_{\rm slot}^{2N}Z^{B_{\rm sel}\delta},
\tag{A.50}
\]
using \(NF\le2W_q\le2Z^{B_{\rm sel}}\), with \(2^\delta\) in the constant.

The actual ideal-ball count gives
\[
\#\{F\in\mathrm{selectedProducts}(q)\}\le256W_q.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_F\frac{g_q(F)}{W_q}
 \ll_{\delta,N}K_{\rm slot}^{2N}Z^{B_{\rm sel}\delta}.
\tag{A.51}
\]
All these weights are nonnegative. Multiply the common nonnegative budget in (A.48) by (A.51). The exponent fits because
\[
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+B_{\rm sel}\delta
 =\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
   +\frac{B_{\rm sel}\varepsilon}{2(B_{\rm sel}+1)}
 \le\varepsilon.
\]
This proves (A.12).


### C.5. Exact first source, whole kernels and allocation normalizers


Fix $U>1$, $H_0=U^M$, a finite slot set $I$, $P_i=U^{w_i}$ and

$$
b_i(\mathfrak p)=\nu_i(\mathfrak p)W(q_{\mathfrak p}/P_i)
       (q_{\mathfrak p}/P_i)^{-\sigma_i+iv_i}.
$$

Each relative $\nu_i$ retains both defining zero sets. Pools contain all support primes in the identity ray class and may overlap. Actual affine input has $\sigma_i=33/50$, $\operatorname{supp}W\subset[1,2]$. Put $\chi_z(n)=\eta(n)\chi_n(m^6Az)$ with original zeros, and

$$
L_z(p,X;t)=\sum_{n\ne0}\chi_z(n)q_n^{it}p(q_n/X),\qquad
 V=X_1X_2\prod_{i\in I}P_i.
$$

The energy to reduce is

<a id="sr:energy"></a>

$$
\qquad\text{(115)}
 E_X=\frac1V\sum_{\substack{z\ne0\\\operatorname{keep}(z)}}
 \Phi(q_z/H_0)
 \left|L_z(p_1,X_1;t)L_z(p_2,X_2;t)
       \prod_i\sum_{\mathfrak p\in\mathcal P_i}
         b_i(\mathfrak p)\chi_z(\mathfrak p)q_{\mathfrak p}^{it}\right|^2 .
$$

Use real nonnegative $\Phi$ (or $\Re\Phi$ in the complex-profile convention). Keep the actual natural predicate and the same fixed \(Q_{\rm int}\) satisfying §2, including \(Q_{\rm int}\subseteq(72)\); later zero bins do not replace it.

Fix bounded geometric ranges: \(0<M_{\min}\le M\le M_{\max}\),
nonnegative slot widths with bounded total, and four positive ordinary scales
\(X_1,X_2,Y_1,Y_2\) with bounded clipped logarithms and
\(X_1X_2=Y_1Y_2\). Empty annuli contribute zero. Every nonempty
ordinary annulus in the source has its central scale bounded below by
\(4/9\), so subunit normalization costs a fixed constant. The reference
rectangles may have an empty factor; this is used in LOW below.

<a id="sr:initial-scales"></a>

The actual application is the root cone \(P+LS\le B<1\) of
Appendix C.10, including all genuine prefix shortenings. The more
restrictive historical conditions \(.41M\le\log_U X_i\le.44M\)
are not used in the identities that follow. Define the literal difference

<a id="sr:comparison"></a>
\[
D(l_1,l_2)=p_1(q_{l_1}/X_1)p_2(q_{l_2}/X_2)
          -p_1(q_{l_1}/Y_1)p_2(q_{l_2}/Y_2).
\tag{117}
\]
The rectangles have the same product, whole character, masks and slots.
Their two profiles remain independent. To treat original profiles
\(f_1,f_2\) and independent original heights \(t_1,t_2\), choose
the common whole-product height \(t=t_0\), with \(|t_0|\le V_{\rm ht}\) as in (S6) and set
\[
 p_j(x)=f_j(x)x^{i(t_j-t)},\qquad
 L_z(f_j,X_j;t_j)=X_j^{i(t_j-t)}L_z(p_j,X_j;t).
\tag{117a}
\]
The original energy is unchanged by its outside unit-modulus phase.
Use these same raised profiles \(p_j\) on both rectangles in (117),
retaining the outside phase belonging to the original \(X_j\).
Equivalently, the unraised reference with heights \(t_j\) is multiplied
by the exact scalar
\[
 (X_1/Y_1)^{i(t_1-t)}(X_2/Y_2)^{i(t_2-t)}.
\tag{117b}
\]
Thus the principal Mellin products cancel literally: after raising,
the two terms have the same common norm power and the same profile
integrals, while \(X_1X_2=Y_1Y_2\). Equating the two independent
heights is neither necessary nor allowed. Derivatives of the raised
profiles have polynomial cost in both height differences, paid by the
full logarithmic kernels and the common finite profile control. Prefix
extractions retain their exact unit phases. Keep the whole rectangle
difference until positive child norms form.

For actual-pool tuples $\mathbf l=(p_i,l_1,l_2)$ on the union of plain annuli, put $J(\mathbf l)=(\prod p_i)l_1l_2$. With common puncture $R$ and squarefree seed $s$, define

<a id="sr:beta"></a>

$$
\qquad\text{(118)}
 \beta_{R,s}(J)=
 \sum_{\substack{\mathbf l\\J(\mathbf l)=J}}
 \left(\prod_i b_i(p_i)\right)D(l_1,l_2)
 \mathbf1_{(J,R)=1}\mathbf1_{s\mid J}.
$$

Initially $R=s=1$. Zeros remain zero; later masks/divisors are actual extractions, not new conditions on plain quotients.

<a id="sr:comparison-bound"></a>
**Reference inlet.** The comparison bound is supplied with its actual
geometric hypotheses, after the root is classified in Appendix C.10.
LOW sets one reference scale to \(2/9\); support in
\([1/4,9/4]\) makes that factor exactly zero, so no reference
estimate is required. HIGH uses the general common-product,
two-orientation estimate proved in Appendix C.4, with the reference
interval and root reserves proved in Appendix C.9 and C.10(20)–(26).
Those arguments retain the natural reflection masks and polynomial
height/profile bounds. They do not use the old narrow numerical rectangle
or an already improved endpoint.

#### The first exact Poisson source

Let $E_D$ be the energy of the whole difference in [(117)](#sr:comparison). Positivity gives

<a id="sr:positive-comparison"></a>

$$
\qquad\text{(119)}
 E_X\le2E_D+2E_Y.
$$

Enlarge only $E_D$ to all rows; never transform the keep predicate.

Fix nonnegative smooth $\Psi$ supported in $[-1,b_\Phi+1]$, $\Psi\ge1$ on $[0,b_\Phi]$, so $0\le\Phi\le\mathcal D(\Phi)\Psi$ for $x\ge0$. Before live subsets/labels, expand [(118)](#sr:beta) in the full lattice square and extract complete common support $Ca,Db$, $(a,b)=(ab,CD)=1$. Define

$$
c=\log_Uq_C,\ d=\log_Uq_D,\ p=\log_Uq_{\operatorname{rad}(CD)},\
 A_0=\log_UV.
$$

Let $r$ contain nonzero net common sextic exponents, length $R_1$, primitive character $\xi_r$. Expand the remaining mask by $e\mid\operatorname{rad}(CD)/r$, length $E_1$, so $R_1+E_1\le p$. For actual allocated convolutions $A_C,A_D$, nonzero frequency gives

<a id="sr:first-poisson"></a>

$$
\qquad\text{(120)}
 \begin{aligned}
 \frac{H_0}{Vq_e\sqrt{q_r}}\sum_{h\ne0}\mathfrak g_{\xi_r}(r,h)
 \sum_{(a,b)=1}&\frac{A_C(a)\overline{A_D(b)}}{\sqrt{q_aq_b}}
 \tau_C(a)\overline{\tau_D(b)}R(a,b)\\
 &\times\mathfrak g(a,h)\overline{\mathfrak g(b,-h)}
 \widehat\Psi\!\left(\frac{H_0q_h}{q_eq_rq_aq_b}\right).
 \end{aligned}
$$

One orientation is $\tau_C(a)=\tau(a)\chi_a(er)\overline{\xi_r(a)}$, $\tau_D(b)=\tau(b)\chi_b(er)\xi_r(b)$. Keep in $A_C$ the exact frozen CRT scalar, $\mu(e)$ and fixed character values, including zeros. Convention-independently, if $f_{C,D,e}(x)$ is the actual active common character times both residual zero-extended characters at $ex$, define

$$
\mathcal T_{C,D,e}(h)=\sum_{x\bmod rab}
            f_{C,D,e}(x)e(hx/(rab)).
$$

Poisson multiplies it by $H_0/(q_eq_rq_aq_b)$; CRT defines all displayed factors simultaneously, preserving unit phases. Three Gauss sums restore $\sqrt{q_rq_aq_b}$ and central normalization gives $1/V$. The cross factor $\chi_a(br)\overline{\chi_b(ar)}\overline{\xi_r(ab)}$ gives $R(a,b)$ by reciprocity. This proves the formula with nonunit zeros; changing orientation conjugates the whole character.

On retained smooth frequency dyads define $\mathcal B_q$ as $V$ times the normalized block [(120)](#sr:first-poisson), removing its $1/V$ once. Include all common labels, inactive subsets and dyadic coordinates. Its normalized contribution is $\mathcal B_q/V$ and physical mass is

<a id="sr:physical-mass"></a>

$$
\qquad\text{(121)}
 \mathcal M_{\rm phys}=\sum_q|\mathcal B_q|
   =\left|\sum_q\zeta_q\mathcal B_q\right|,\qquad
 \zeta_q=\begin{cases}|\mathcal B_q|/\mathcal B_q,&\mathcal B_q\ne0,\\
 0,&\mathcal B_q=0.\end{cases}
$$

First labels thus stay in one joint sum, without an extra count.

The powerful zero-frequency argument of §[7.2.6](#first-poisson-from-plain-products-to-gauss-polynomials), now with full product norm $V$, gives $O(H_0U^\epsilon\mathcal H_J)$ after divisor allocations and central $1/V$, retaining every mask.

The nominal first frequency length is

<a id="sr:first-scale"></a>

**(122)** is [(76)](#cf:eq:D.12) under $(A,R,E,m)=(A_0,R_1,E_1,M)$: $K_0=2A_0-c-d+R_1+E_1-M$.

Retain whole dyads through each outer box's maximum scale with enclosure $\delta_1<\xi$. Discarded genuine arguments are $\ge U^{\xi/4}$ after fixed support errors. Use $|\mathfrak g(a,h)|\le\sqrt{q_a}$ and polynomial counts, fixing raw cost before Schwartz order. For every fixed $L>0$, 

<a id="sr:first-remainder"></a>

$$
\qquad\text{(123)}
 E_D\le\mathcal D(\Phi)\{\mathcal M_{\rm phys}/V+
 C\mathcal H_JH_0(U^\epsilon+U^{-L})\}.
$$

<a id="sr:initial-reduction"></a>
**First-source reduction.** If the chosen comparison satisfies
\(E_Y\ll\mathcal D(\Phi)\mathcal H_J
(1+|t_1|+|t_2|+|t|+\max_i|v_i|)^J U^{M+\epsilon}\), or is
identically zero, then

<a id="sr:initial-inequality"></a>
\[
 E_X\le2\mathcal D(\Phi)\mathcal M_{\rm phys}/V+
 C\mathcal D(\Phi)\mathcal H_J
 (1+|t_1|+|t_2|+|t|+\max_i|v_i|)^J U^{M+\epsilon}.
\tag{124}
\]
**Proof.** Combine (119) with (123) and the stated comparison bound.
The displayed Poisson identity is a finite expansion followed by the
exact arithmetic Poisson formula of Appendix A.6, so it imposes no
numerical affine interval on an ordinary exponent. On every actual
root of Appendix C.10, its full product volume is at most \(Z\),
and the support cap is at most \((9/4)^2 2^N\) times that volume.
All extracted quotients only shorten these supports. Thus the raw
counts, Gauss bounds and profile derivatives in (123) have one fixed
polynomial envelope. Fix that exponent before the Schwartz tail order.
The zero-frequency proof in Appendix A.7.2.6 uses the same product
volume and powerful-prime condition and retains every zero mask; it
has no lower interval condition on either ordinary exponent.

The full kernels (125) absorb the independent height differences at a
polynomial cost. The geometric mesh precedes the finite slot dictionary;
after it is fixed, take the finite maximum over its subsets and the four
plain derivative pairs. Assign half the loss to the comparison and
remainder and absorb the finite logarithmic partitions in the remainder.
These choices give one threshold for every live shortening, mask,
ordinary profile and independent height. The precise LOW/HIGH
comparisons are discharged in Appendix C.10, completing the conditional
inlet in the full source proof. ∎
